hero.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers credited Flock Safety license plate reader cameras with leading to an arrest in a Vero Beach homicide case after the system tracked a suspect to a West Virginia motel, sparking a growing debate among Treasure Coast residents over privacy and oversight. Flowers described the case as a cold-blooded murder that triggered a multi-state manhunt. The Flock Safety system is a nationwide network of cameras connected to a searchable law enforcement database.

Many residents welcomed the technology after the arrest. Larry, a Treasure Coast resident, said he thinks the cameras are a good thing for keeping criminals out of people's lives. Meghan Ford, a Treasure Coast visitor, said she sees value in the system for finding people who have committed horrible crimes or locating missing children.

Others expressed concern about privacy and control of the technology. Stuart resident Michael Maslak questioned where the line should be drawn on privacy. Recent reports indicate some officers have misused the Flock Safety system to track romantic partners. In response, Flock Safety announced changes requiring searches to include a case number and mandating that all agencies use a new audit system designed to flag suspicious activity.

hero.body:
A Fort Pierce man faces a manslaughter charge after a 34-year-old man died following a BB gun shooting on August 22, 2026, in the 2900 block of Avenue G. Fort Pierce Police officers responded to reports of a gunshot victim and found the 34-year-old male suffering from an injury. The victim was transported to Lawnwood Hospital, where he later died.

The initial investigation revealed that a group of males had been shooting a BB gun at trees when the suspect, Jabari Cowart, 36, asked to use the BB gun. During the interaction, Cowart reportedly pointed the BB gun in the victim's direction and fired. Shortly thereafter, the victim collapsed.

Cowart was subsequently charged with manslaughter and taken to the St. Lucie County Jail. The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation by the Fort Pierce Police Department.

The shooting occurred on a Saturday in a residential area of Fort Pierce. Police have not released the identity of the victim.

hero.angle: Lead with Martin County School District's ban on fake squishy toys in classrooms following a CPSC safety alert, and outline the specific risks prompting parents to check their kids' toys.

hero.body:
The Martin County School District announced it will exclude fake squishy toys from classroom activities after the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission issued a safety alert about the products. The district cautioned parents about the risks these toys may pose to children.

The warning comes in response to the federal agency's alert about counterfeit squishy toys. The district made the announcement on Monday.

Education leaders are encouraging parents to pay close attention to the risks these toys may pose to children. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission issued the safety alert that prompted the school district's response.

The Martin County School District serves students throughout the county including Stuart, Jensen Beach, Palm City, Hobe Sound, and Port Salerno. Parents can monitor the situation through the district's communications channels.

cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is asking for public help to locate Racqueal Annalessa Martin, a Fort Pierce woman who has been missing for 10 days. On Aug. 14, Martin reportedly went to Love's Truck Stop in Fort Pierce and got a ride from a truck driver to another Love's Truck Stop in Memphis, Tennessee, according to SLCSO. She has been reported missing since.

Martin was last seen wearing a black and green shirt with get money written on it, black and white shorts, and black flip-flops while carrying a dark-colored bag. She is a black female standing at 5 feet 6 inches tall, weighing approximately 140 pounds with hazel colored hair and brown eyes.

Anyone with information is encouraged to call 911 or contact Detective Corporal Bogner at 772-462-3230.

cards.body:
Fort Pierce began enforcing two-hour parking limits in parts of downtown in July, issuing $50 citations to drivers who exceed the limit and $100 for repeat offenses. City officials said the initiative aims to increase parking turnover, improve traffic flow, and make it easier for visitors to find available spaces. The limits are enforced Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m.

Beryl Muise, owner of Notions Potions, said the two-hour limit has benefited her business by helping customers find parking spots without driving in circles. Muise said the turnover helps customers who are handicapped and cannot walk from the two free parking garages nearby. One restaurant declined to comment on camera but told officials two hours is not long enough for the lunch rush, especially with limited parking in front of the establishment.

Muise said weekends are less congested because offices such as the public defender's office and title companies have employees downtown only Monday through Friday. She said the weekend parking situation benefits both retail and restaurants. The city of Fort Pierce has not yet responded to inquiries about the number of citations issued.
cards.headline: Fort Pierce two-hour downtown parking enforcement draws mixed reaction from businesses
cards.teaser: Fort Pierce began issuing citations in July for drivers who exceed two-hour parking limits in parts of downtown. Retail stores report easier customer access, but at least one restaurant says the limit is too short for the lunch rush.

cards.body:
Residents whose homes were damaged by an EF-0 tornado in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening say their phones alerted them to a tornado warning roughly 20 minutes after the storm had already hit. Carol Cadotte, who had parts of her roof ripped off when the tornado started near her home, said the delayed alert raised safety concerns. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," Cadotte said.

The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club, with peak winds of 75 mph. The tornado traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes before moving over the St. Lucie River as a waterspout, then returning onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said the tornado was difficult to detect because it was a landspout that formed along the leading edge of a thunderstorm rather than from a rotating supercell. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said.

The tornado caused fence and roof damage in the Southbend area and near Bay St. Lucie, but no homes were destroyed and there were no injuries. Allison Rogers, who lives off Southbend Boulevard across from Jessica Clinton Park, had her fence blown down and her shed damaged. Cadotte said her house had survived all previous hurricanes without losing anything. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," Cadotte said.
cards.headline: Port St. Lucie tornado victims say emergency alerts arrived 20 minutes after storm passed
cards.teaser: Residents whose homes were damaged by an EF-0 tornado in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening say their phones alerted them to a tornado warning roughly 20 minutes after the storm had already hit.

hero.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed Monday that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path. Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas. The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club, and produced minimal structural damage including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations.

The tornado moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m. The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, Ulrich said, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph. The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado.

Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it was not raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through. This was more of boundary interactions from those daily afternoon showers and thunderstorms that we receive, and lately it has been abnormally warm, Ulrich said. The more heat you have, the more vigorous those boundary collisions are going to be.

Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed. No injuries were reported from the tornado, officials confirmed. The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event. While landspouts are more common during summer months in Florida, any one location experiencing a tornado remains historically rare.

An EF0 tornado touched down in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood, leaving some homes damaged and residents recounting the frightening experience. Resident Allison Rogers described the terrifying noises she heard during the storm. 'It sounded like there was a hurricane outside the window, right, because I've heard those noises before and things like that, but it was just a swoosh, and it was just so scary to hear,' Rogers said.

Rogers admitted she was scared as she watched the twister from her home. 'Absolutely, I stood there for a good minute before I even thought about grabbing my phone because you could see the twister in the street. Is it going to hit the windows? There's metal everywhere; it was pretty scary,' Rogers said. Her home lost its fence and shed but never lost power. Another resident, Debbie Mastrolillo, said her home was untouched by the storm. 'Our house, it's 637, did not even get touched. Nothing!' Mastrolillo said.

Aron Christiansen, who lives around the corner, said his roof was damaged during the tornado. 'I looked out my window and we had a bunch of dark clouds over there and I saw a bunch of white and I thought that's a lot of birds and I look closer and it's debris and I'm trying to hustle my dogs into my bedroom and ten seconds later it went through and what we're left with is a big mess,' Christiansen said. The tornado also moved over the St. Lucie River, where one viewer captured video of it as a waterspout.
cards.headline: Port St. Lucie residents describe frightening moments as EF0 tornado swept through neighborhood
cards.teaser: Residents in a Port St. Lucie neighborhood recounted the terrifying experience of watching an EF0 tornado tear through their community Sunday evening, with some homes losing fences and sheds while others escaped damage entirely.

Aron Christiansen spent the morning pulling debris out of his pool after already retrieving furniture from the bottom. Video from a neighbor's camera captured the moment his patio broke apart during the storm. Half of the patio is now out on the curb, set to be salvaged for recycling. 'I looked out the windows last night, saw a bunch of debris flying. I thought it was birds at first; they were white, so I thought they might be ibises. I looked closer, and there's debris, and had about 10 seconds before it hit our house,' Christiansen said.

Janelle Pierre-Louis said she was surprised by the amount of damage to her backyard foliage after dealing with damage at the front of her house first. 'My front door caved in; our door is kind of old. Dirt came through the cracks. It was a hot mess,' Pierre-Louis said. Around the corner, Mitch Brewer had debris piled out front, most of it from a shed he had tied down. 'It looks like it caught some heavy updrafts and left,' Brewer said.

Marlene Torres was in a good mood Sunday night before returning home to find the storm had moved through her neighborhood. 'I had just come back from Jensen Beach celebrating my birthday, which is today,' Torres said. 'I came home and witnessed the tornado.' Her home was not damaged, but she needed an electrician to fix her meter. 'I'm the only one with no electricity because my power was more damaged than other folks in the area, so that is the situation, but I can't complain; it could be worse,' Torres said.

hero.body:
The National Weather Service confirmed that an EF0 tornado touched down Sunday evening in St. Lucie County, damaging about 20 to 30 homes along a 2.1-mile path. Will Ulrich, warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service Melbourne office, announced the findings Monday morning during a press conference at Jessica Clinton Park following a damage survey of the affected areas.

The tornado, classified as a landspout, first touched down around 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitching Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, close to the Tarpon Bay Yacht Club. It produced minimal structural damage, including roof damage, soffit damage and pool enclosures lifted from their foundations. The tornado then moved over the St. Lucie River, where it became a waterspout for approximately five to seven minutes, meandering slowly from north to south over the water before moving back onshore in the Bay St. Lucie community around 6:20 p.m.

The strongest wind gusts likely occurred in the Bay St. Lucie community, where the tornado caused numerous downed trees and large branches, along with damage to well-built homes with tile roofs from winds of 65 to 75 mph. The tornado continued west into Port St. Lucie communities near the Southbend area, where it caused discontinuous damage including downed trees, blown-over fences, and damaged or destroyed pool screen enclosures before dissipating. The entire event lasted approximately 14 to 15 minutes, making it unusually long for this type of tornado. Most of the damage was classified as minor, with approximately 20 to 30 percent of roof covers removed from some homes, though no homes were destroyed.

No injuries were reported from the tornado. Ulrich explained that landspouts form differently than traditional tornadoes, developing closer to the surface along the leading edge of thunderstorm updrafts rather than from mesocyclones. Residents reported it wasn't raining during the tornado itself, with heavy rain arriving only after the tornado passed through. The National Weather Service worked alongside the City of Port St. Lucie Emergency Management and St. Lucie County Emergency Management to conduct interviews with residents and piece together the timeline of the event.

Residents whose homes were damaged by an EF-0 tornado in Port St. Lucie Sunday evening say their phones alerted them to a tornado warning roughly 20 minutes after the storm had already hit. Carol Cadotte, who had parts of her roof ripped off when the tornado started near her home, said the delayed alert raised safety concerns. "Our phones went off, and we looked at each other like, you're kidding me, right? 20 minutes later, that's something's wrong with that picture," Cadotte said.

The National Weather Service confirmed the tornado touched down at 6:10 p.m. near Southeast Kitchen Cove Lane and Southeast Morningside Boulevard, near the Tarpon Bay Club, with peak winds of 75 mph. The tornado traveled a little more than two miles over 14 to 15 minutes before moving over the St. Lucie River as a waterspout, then returning onshore near the Bay St. Lucie community at about 6:20 p.m. Will Ulrich, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service, said the tornado was difficult to detect because it was a landspout that formed along the leading edge of a thunderstorm rather than from a rotating supercell. "The problem with landspouts is that the circulations aren't particularly strong, such that we can very easily see it on radar. We know that there's a weak circulation, but we see weak circulations all the time, so that doesn't necessarily always lead to a tornado," Ulrich said.

The tornado caused fence and roof damage in the Southbend area and near Bay St. Lucie, but no homes were destroyed and there were no injuries. Allison Rogers, who lives off Southbend Boulevard across from Jessica Clinton Park, had her fence blown down and her shed damaged. Cadotte said her house had survived all previous hurricanes without losing anything. "My house is old, but it made it through all the hurricanes. It never lost anything ever. Through all the crazy ones we've had. This was five minutes, and my roof just peeled off like a Band-Aid," Cadotte said.
